title: How Does Your Heart Actually Work?
hook: Put your hand on your chest. That steady thump is a muscle that never stops working, not even while you sleep. But what is it actually doing?

beats.narration: Put your hand on your chest. That steady thump is a muscle that never stops working, not even while you sleep. But what is it actually doing?
Every beat follows the same precise routine. And a tiny group of cells is secretly in charge of all of it.
Inside, your heart has four rooms called chambers. The two on top, the atria, collect blood. The two below, the ventricles, push it out.
The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to your lungs to pick up fresh oxygen. Then the left side pumps that oxygen-rich blood out to your whole body.
Between the chambers are valves, like little one-way doors. In a healthy heart, they make sure blood only ever flows forward.
So who's in charge? A tiny group of pacemaker cells, only about 1 percent of heart cells, fires an electrical spark that starts every single beat.
At rest, an adult heart beats about 72 times a minute. Each full beat takes less than a second, about 0.8 seconds from start to finish.
Here's the wild part: your heart feeds itself between beats. Its own blood supply flows mainly while it relaxes, not while it squeezes.
So every thump is a perfectly timed squeeze and relax, sending blood on a nonstop round trip. Pretty amazing for one muscle. Stay curious!
